Convex hull description of hypersimplex and standard positive weighted welfare support
correctness.rationale: For at most three unit-approval voters, classify candidate approval types as zero, full, e_i singletons and p_i=1−e_i pairs. A Pareto-optimal size-k committee cannot select any type dominated by an omitted candidate. If no singleton is selected or all pairs are selected, it consists of top-k candidates by (1,1,1) score. Otherwise select singleton e_j and omit pair p_j: no-improving-swap forces all selected singletons to be e_j and every omitted pair to be p_j; (2,1,1) with the weight 2 on coordinate j orders all remaining types and supports that committee. Each of the four universal score maxima is Pareto efficient since weights are strictly positive, and also fractionally Pareto efficient since the cardinality-k hypersimplex is the convex hull of integral committees. Conversely fractional Pareto implies integral. Boundaries k=0, k=|C| and absent voters are included. Independently enumerated all 256 subsets of the eight approval types and every feasible k, comparing integral Pareto frontiers to the four-weight union over 5,822 unique utility-profile checks, no disagreements. The original source checker also enumerates capacities 0..2 per type for 3^8 profiles; the finite test is corroboration of the infinite-candidate argument.
residual_risks: The theorem is special to additive 0/1 approval and at most three voters.
Positive score tie-breaking may yield several committees, all of which are efficient; no unique winner claimed.

value.rationale: A strong unbounded-candidate structural theorem reducing a difficult Pareto frontier to four election-independent weighted scores in a natural small-voter domain. The exact equality of integral and fractional Pareto frontiers improves on general fractional support characterization and yields simple O(|C|log|C|) membership checking; it is not a finite dataset recomputation.
residual_risks: Only for at most three unit-approval voters and fixed-cardinality committees.

limitations: No generalization to 4 voters, nonlinear utilities, candidate costs or knapsack constraints.
General positive weights may vary by instance; the special claim concerns these four fixed vectors only.
